content: Thumb sucking is the repetitive act of placing the thumb into the mouth and rhythmically sucking on it for an extended period. This behavior can also involve other accessible parts of the body, such as the big toe, and is often perceived as soothing and therapeutic for the individual. Thumb sucking is most commonly observed in infants and young children. Babies and children engage in sucking behaviors, including the use of pacifiers, as a natural reflex to self-soothe. This reflex is entirely normal during early childhood development. While some adults may also engage in thumb sucking, it is rarely done in public due to embarrassment or social stigma, leading to the misconception that adults do not engage in this behavior at all. Adults who suck their thumbs often do so privately to avoid judgment or ridicule. Thumb sucking can begin as early as 15 weeks of gestation in the womb or within the first few months after birth. Before 12 weeks of gestation, the fetus has webbed digits, making thumb sucking impossible. Most children naturally stop thumb sucking by the age of five, and it is uncommon for the habit to persist into adulthood. Some individuals may suck on both thumbs or their fingers, and finger sucking is considered similar to thumb sucking in terms of its effects and treatment, though it is less common. Dental Problems Thumb sucking can lead to dental developmental issues if it persists beyond a certain age. To discourage thumb sucking, some parents have historically used methods such as applying hot sauce or sour substances to their child’s thumb. However, these practices are not recommended by the American Dental Association (ADA) or the American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry. In the 1950s, some parents resorted to having sharp prongs, known as hay-rakes, cemented to their child’s teeth to prevent thumb sucking. Most children stop sucking their thumbs, pacifiers, or other objects on their own between the ages of two and four. No significant harm is typically done to their teeth or jaw unless the habit continues after the eruption of permanent teeth. Concerns arise if thumb sucking persists beyond the ages of six to eight, as it may alter the shape of the oral cavity or dentition. The ADA offers the following recommendations to address thumb sucking: Praise children for not sucking their thumbs rather than scolding them when they do. If thumb sucking is a response to insecurity or a need for comfort, address the underlying cause of the anxiety and provide reassurance to the child. If the habit stems from boredom, engage the child in a fun activity to redirect their attention. Involve older children in choosing a method to stop thumb sucking. Pediatric dentists can provide encouragement and explain the potential consequences of prolonged thumb sucking on dental health. If other methods fail, gently remind the child of their habit by bandaging the thumb or placing a sock or glove on the hand at night. Best Practices Recommendations The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) states that most children engage in thumb or finger sucking at some point in early life. Concern arises only if the habit continues beyond the ages of six to eight or if it affects the shape of the mouth and the alignment of teeth. The ADA emphasizes that while sucking is a natural reflex, it can lead to skeletal and dental alignment issues during and after the eruption of permanent teeth. Thumb Sucking and Sexuality Sigmund Freud regarded thumb sucking as a form of sexual expression and used it as a basis for studying infantile sexuality. Intense thumb sucking can fully absorb a child’s attention, sometimes leading to sleep or, in rare cases, a motor reaction resembling an orgasm. Additionally, thumb sucking is sometimes accompanied by the stimulation of other sensitive areas of the body, such as the genitals, which may lead to a progression from thumb sucking to masturbation. In 1919, Dr. Galant published a case in Neurologisches Zentralblatt describing a young woman who continued thumb sucking into adulthood and likened the satisfaction derived from it to sexual gratification. Media References The 2005 film Thumbsucker, directed by Mike Mills, explores the life of a 17-year-old teenager who struggles with the habit of thumb sucking. The movie is based on the 1999 novel of the same name by Walter Kirn. In Walt Disney Studio’s 1973 animated film Robin Hood, the character Prince John is depicted as an adult who sucks his thumb.
